outages.cause: Rolling and emergency blackouts after Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, including a large-scale attack on Nov 20 and further strikes reported on subsequent days, including overnight and on the morning of Wednesday, Nov 25. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy, as reported Wednesday morning by Interfax-Ukraine, Ukrainska Pravda, and UNN, said Russia had again attacked energy facilities overnight and on Wednesday morning, targeting power plants and electricity transmission and distribution substations, and that the attacks caused new power outages in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, and Kharkiv regions. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform, said a significant number of energy facilities important to regional electricity supply had been damaged over the past day, that the situation remained especially difficult in Dnipropetrovsk region and Zaporizhzhia region, that after large-scale outages in Zaporizhzhia electricity supply had been partially restored, and that emergency outages were in effect in Dnipropetrovsk region. The Energy Ministry, as reported by the same Wednesday accounts, and UNN citing the IAEA, said the temporarily occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant had lost its external power supply and switched to diesel generators. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform, said that because of damage to energy equipment, restrictions would be in effect until the end of Wednesday in some regions: capacity-limitation schedules for industry and hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3 queues for all categories of consumers. Earlier Tuesday evening accounts, including UNN, kurs.com.ua, 24tv.ua, and UNIAN, citing Ukrenergo, had already said planned outage schedules would again be in effect around the clock on Wednesday, Nov 25, in parts of the country, with hourly outages of 0.5 to 3 queues for all categories of consumers and capacity-limitation schedules for industry
outages.affected: Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform at 11:06 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (3:06 a.m. CT), said that as of Wednesday morning, as a result of Russian attacks over the past day that damaged a significant number of energy facilities important to regional electricity supply, there were de-energized consumers in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, and Kharkiv regions. The same report said the situation remained especially difficult in Dnipropetrovsk region and Zaporizhzhia region, that after large-scale outages in Zaporizhzhia electricity supply had been partially restored, and that emergency outages were in effect in Dnipropetrovsk region, with restoration work continuing. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform, also said that because of damage to energy equipment, restrictions would be in effect until the end of the day in some regions: capacity-limitation schedules for industry, and hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3 queues for all categories of consumers, and that current schedules should be checked on the official pages of the distribution-system operator. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy, as reported by Interfax-Ukraine at 11:49 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (3:49 a.m. CT), by Ukrainska Pravda at 10:42 a.m. Wednesday (2:42 a.m. CT), and by UNN at 8:35 a.m. Wednesday (12:35 a.m. CT), said Russia had again attacked energy facilities overnight and on Wednesday morning, targeting power plants and electricity transmission and distribution substations, and that the attacks caused new power outages in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, and Kharkiv regions. Those reports, citing the ministry, said repair and restoration work was ongoing in all affected regions, but that repeated attacks and constant air-raid alerts were significantly complicating the work and delaying restoration; that as of Wednesday morning the situation remained most difficult in the Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions, where the attacks damaged a significant number of energy facilities essential to electricity supply; and that additional grid restrictions were being applied to prevent emergencies caused by equipment overload. The same Energy Ministry accounts, and UNN citing the IAEA, said the temporarily occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant had lost its external power supply and switched to diesel generators, the plant's 17th loss of external power since the beginning of 2026. UNN said it was the plant's 28th such blackout overall. The IAEA, as quoted by UNN, said the plant was relying on emergency diesel generators to perform essential nuclear safety and security functions after losing all off-site power for the 28th time during the conflict, and that the connection to the plant's sole remaining external power line, Ferosplavna-1, was lost at 5:28 a.m. local time on Nov 25 (9:28 p.m. CT Tuesday, Nov 24). UNN, citing the ministry, also said that on Nov 25, hourly electricity outage schedules were in effect in most regions of Ukraine, while capacity restriction schedules applied to industry. An earlier Tuesday evening Ukrenergo statement, as reported by UNN at 5:02 p.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (9:02 a.m. CT), by kurs.com.ua, and by 24tv.ua, and by UNIAN in a report updated at 9:17 p.m. Tuesday (1:17 p.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), had already said that on Wednesday, Nov 25, planned outages would again be in effect around the clock in parts of the country, with hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3 queues for all categories of consumers, corresponding to about two to 12 hours without electricity, and capacity-limitation schedules for industry. No official nationwide customer count was found as of 6:00 AM CT Wednesday, Nov 25 (2:00 p.m. Wednesday, EET).

outages.place: Odesa and parts of Odesa and Bolhrad districts
outages.cause: Repeated Russian attacks on high-voltage transmission networks and other energy facilities critical to the region, including a strike on a DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi energy facility on the morning of Nov 20, and further damage reported over Nov 24-25. Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper, as reported by Ukrinform at 12:43 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25, said that over the past day Russian attacks had again damaged energy equipment in Odesa region. DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, as reported Wednesday morning by Odessa Life in an update at 7:54 a.m., said stabilization outages would be applied in Odesa and Odesa region on Wednesday, Nov 25, on Ukrenergo's command, and that schedules could be adjusted if Ukrenergo's commands changed. The same Odessa Life report, citing the company, also said urgent equipment repairs in Odesa's Peresypskyi district would leave that area without electricity from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Wednesday, as previously announced
outages.affected: Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper, as reported by Ukrinform at 12:43 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (4:43 a.m. CT), said that over the past day Russian attacks had again damaged energy equipment in Odesa region, and that about 9,000 subscribers in parts of Odesa and Bolhrad districts of the region were temporarily without electricity. Kiper, as reported by Ukrinform, also said that during the previous evening's attack a DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi production site in the region had been damaged, including 16 units of special-purpose vehicles, and that company employees were not injured. Odessa Life, in a Wednesday report published at 6:42 a.m. and updated at 7:54 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (10:42 p.m. and 11:54 p.m. CT Tuesday, Nov 24), citing DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, said that on Wednesday, Nov 25, stabilization outages would be in effect in Odesa and Odesa region on Ukrenergo's command, that residents should check the schedule for a given address on the company's website, Viber group, or Telegram chatbot, and that if Ukrenergo's commands changed the schedules could also be adjusted. The same report said energy workers would carry out urgent equipment repairs in Odesa's Peresypskyi district, where there would be no electricity from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy and Ukrenergo, in Wednesday morning updates reported by Interfax-Ukraine, Ukrainska Pravda, UNN, and Ukrinform, listed Odesa region among five regions with new power outages after overnight and Wednesday-morning attacks. An earlier Odesa Report article published at 10:02 p.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (2:02 p.m. CT), citing Ukrenergo, had said that on Wednesday hourly outage schedules would be applied throughout the day, that depending on the region electricity may be absent from two to 12 hours a day, and that in Odesa and Odesa district energy workers had already returned to stabilization schedules after difficult emergency repairs, while networks remained vulnerable to overloads. No later official count beyond Kiper's figure of about 9,000 subscribers in parts of Odesa and Bolhrad districts was found as of 6:00 AM CT Wednesday, Nov 25 (2:00 p.m. Wednesday, EET).
outages.updated: Nov 25, 2026, Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper via Ukrinform 12:43 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (= 4:43 a.m. CT), on Russian attacks again damaging energy equipment in Odesa region over the past day, about 9,000 subscribers temporarily without electricity in parts of Odesa and Bolhrad districts, and damage to a DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi production site, including 16 special-purpose vehicles, in the previous evening's attack; DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi via Odessa Life published 6:42 a.m. Wednesday, updated 7:54 a.m. Wednesday (= 10:42 p.m. and 11:54 p.m. CT Tuesday, Nov 24), on Wednesday stabilization outages in Odesa and the region on Ukrenergo's command, with schedules subject to change, and on urgent Peresypskyi district repairs from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.; Energy Ministry and Ukrenergo Wednesday morning updates listing Odesa region among five regions with new outages; earlier Odesa Report 10:02 p.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (= 2:02 p.m. CT); rechecked 6:00 AM CT Wednesday, Nov 25 (2:00 p.m. Wednesday, EET)

outages.place: Dnipro and parts of Dnipropetrovsk region, including Dniprovskyi, Pavlohradskyi, Synelnykivskyi, and Samarivskyi districts
outages.cause: Russian attacks on energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk region, including strikes on Nov 24 and overnight into Nov 25, and a Wednesday, Nov 25, attack on one of DTEK's thermal power plants, which DTEK said had been hit in a massive attack, had stopped generating electricity, and had sustained significant equipment damage, the company's third massive attack on its plants in November alone. DTEK, as reported Wednesday morning by UNN and by 5692.com.ua, said that because of the strikes, homes and part of critical infrastructure were left without electricity, and that by order of Ukrenergo emergency outages were being applied in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Pavlohradskyi, Synelnykivskyi, and Samarivskyi districts, where hourly schedules were not in effect. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform, and Ukraine's Ministry of Energy, as reported by Interfax-Ukraine, Ukrainska Pravda, and UNN, said the situation remained especially difficult in Dnipropetrovsk region, with emergency outages in effect
outages.affected: DTEK, as reported by UNN at 9:51 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (1:51 a.m. CT), said that on Wednesday Russia had carried out a massive attack on one of DTEK's thermal power plants, that the plant had stopped generating electricity, that equipment had been significantly damaged, and that this was already the third massive attack on the company's plants in November alone. The same DTEK statement, as reported by UNN and by 5692.com.ua in a report time-stamped 11:22 a.m. Wednesday (3:22 a.m. CT) on a DTEK update as of 10:26 a.m. Wednesday (2:26 a.m. CT), said that on Tuesday and overnight into Wednesday Russia had again struck energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk region, and that because of those strikes homes and part of critical infrastructure were left without electricity. DTEK said that by order of Ukrenergo, emergency outages were being applied in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Pavlohradskyi, Synelnykivskyi, and Samarivskyi districts, that hourly schedules were not in effect there, that the situation in the region was extremely difficult, that energy workers across the region were working to stabilize it, and that prolonged air-raid alerts were complicating repairs. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform at 11:06 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (3:06 a.m. CT), said the situation remained especially difficult in Dnipropetrovsk region and Zaporizhzhia region, and that emergency outages were in effect in Dnipropetrovsk region, with restoration work continuing. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy, as reported Wednesday morning by Interfax-Ukraine, Ukrainska Pravda, and UNN, likewise said the situation as of Wednesday morning remained most difficult in the Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions, where attacks had damaged a significant number of energy facilities essential to electricity supply, and that additional grid restrictions were being applied to prevent emergencies caused by equipment overload. An earlier Suspilne report published at 7:32 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (11:32 p.m. CT Tuesday, Nov 24), and updated at 7:51 a.m. Wednesday (11:51 p.m. CT Tuesday), citing DTEK, had already said emergency outages were in effect in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianskyi, and Pavlohradskyi districts, where schedules were not being applied. No official customer count was found as of 6:00 AM CT Wednesday, Nov 25 (2:00 p.m. Wednesday, EET).
outages.updated: Nov 25, 2026, DTEK via UNN 9:51 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (= 1:51 a.m. CT), on a massive Wednesday attack that stopped generation at one of DTEK's thermal power plants, with significant equipment damage, the company's third massive plant attack in November, and on emergency outages by Ukrenergo order in Dnipro and the Dniprovskyi, Pavlohradskyi, Synelnykivskyi, and Samarivskyi districts, where schedules were not in effect, after Tuesday and overnight strikes that left homes and part of critical infrastructure without power; the same DTEK update via 5692.com.ua 11:22 a.m. Wednesday (= 3:22 a.m. CT) as of 10:26 a.m. Wednesday (= 2:26 a.m. CT); Ukrenergo via Ukrinform 11:06 a.m. Wednesday (= 3:06 a.m. CT) on emergency outages in Dnipropetrovsk region and an especially difficult situation there; Energy Ministry via Interfax-Ukraine, Ukrainska Pravda, and UNN on the most difficult situation in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions; earlier Suspilne 7:32 a.m. Wednesday, updated 7:51 a.m. (= 11:32 p.m. and 11:51 p.m. CT Tuesday), citing DTEK, including Kamianskyi district among earlier Wednesday emergency-outage areas; rechecked 6:00 AM CT Wednesday, Nov 25 (2:00 p.m. Wednesday, EET), no official customer count found

outages.cause: Damage to energy infrastructure from Russian shelling, according to JSC Zaporizhiaoblenergo. The company's head, Andriy Stasevsky, in a Wednesday morning statement reported by Interfax-Ukraine, said a significant number of consumers in the city of Zaporizhzhia and Zaporizhzhia region had been left without electricity as a result of that damage, and that the emergency response plan for systemic power-grid failures had been activated. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy, as reported Wednesday morning by Interfax-Ukraine, Ukrainska Pravda, and UNN, said the situation as of Wednesday morning remained most difficult in the Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions, where attacks had damaged a significant number of energy facilities essential to electricity supply
outages.affected: JSC Zaporizhiaoblenergo, in a Wednesday morning statement by the company's head, Andriy Stasevsky, as reported by Interfax-Ukraine in Ukrainian at 7:36 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (11:36 p.m. CT Tuesday, Nov 24) and in English at 9:21 a.m. Wednesday (1:21 a.m. CT), said that as a result of damage to energy infrastructure caused by shelling by Russian occupation forces, a significant number of consumers in the city of Zaporizhzhia and Zaporizhzhia region had been left without electricity, that the emergency response plan for systemic power-grid failures had been activated, and that the company was working to restore electricity supply. Censor.NET, in a report time-stamped 7:12 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (11:12 p.m. CT Tuesday), citing Zaporizhzhia regional military administration head Mykhailo Semikin, likewise said that because of damage to energy infrastructure from Russian shelling, part of the residents of Zaporizhzhia region had been left without electricity, and quoted the same Stasevsky statement. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform at 11:06 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (3:06 a.m. CT), said the situation remained especially difficult in Dnipropetrovsk region and Zaporizhzhia region, and that after large-scale outages in Zaporizhzhia electricity supply had been partially restored, with restoration work continuing. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy, as reported Wednesday morning by Interfax-Ukraine, Ukrainska Pravda, and UNN, said the situation as of Wednesday morning remained most difficult in the Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions. Inform.zp.ua, in a report published at 10:12 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (2:12 a.m. CT), citing Zaporizhiaoblenergo, said hourly outage schedules for Zaporizhzhia and the region on Nov 25 had been updated on Ukrenergo's instructions, with the schedule updated at 7:21 a.m. Wednesday (11:21 p.m. CT Tuesday), and published queue-by-queue outage windows that the report said included 30 minutes for switching. No official customer count was found as of 6:00 AM CT Wednesday, Nov 25 (2:00 p.m. Wednesday, EET).

outages.place: Kurdistan Region, including Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Duhok, Bazian, and Chamchamal
outages.cause: Suspected drone attack on the Khor Mor gas field on the night of Nov 8, 2026, which halted gas production that supplies much of the region's electricity generation. Dana Gas, the field's operator, later said the facility had sustained significant damage and could produce no gas
outages.affected: The New Region, in a Nov 23, 2026 report, said gas production at the Khor Mor field was expected to resume in the coming days after a Monday meeting of delegations from Erbil and Baghdad with the field's operator, Dana Gas; that, according to information acquired by The New Region, the outcome of the meeting was positive, with Dana Gas set to resume gas production in the next two to three days; and that a source at the field told The New Region that all employees at Khor Mor had returned to work, that Dana Gas was set to release a statement on the resumption of operations in the near future, that efforts to repair the damaged sections were also expected to begin soon, and that production was expected to resume within the next 48 hours in areas unaffected by the attack. Omed Ahmed, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Region's electricity ministry, told The New Region on Monday that electricity generation at power stations was expected to resume within hours of gas production restarting, with supply gradually increasing, but that it could take up to 24 hours of normal operations for electricity production to return to pre-attack levels. Those reports did not say that Khor Mor production or pre-attack electricity supply had already resumed. An earlier Nov 22, 2026 report by The New Region had said the Monday meeting was planned to discuss resuming production, that Dana Gas was expected to insist on security guarantees against further attacks, and that if an agreement were reached on Monday, a specialized Turkish company would begin repairs estimated to take six days. Kurdistan24, in a Nov 22, 2026 report, said the Nov 8 drone attack in Sulaimani province caused a large fire and stopped gas production entirely, with no casualties, and that the stoppage cut 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts of electricity in the Kurdistan Region and reduced power-supply hours by five to six hours a day. That account is consistent with earlier official figures: Al Jazeera, on Nov 9, citing Iraqi and Kurdish officials and the official Iraqi News Agency, said the attack left more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region without power and, citing Omed Ahmed, that it suspended gas supply to power plants in Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal, and Duhok and knocked between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts off the grid. Rudaw later quoted Ahmed as saying authorities had increased generation from approximately 1,000 megawatts immediately after the attack to 1,550 megawatts, of which 50 megawatts were reserved for essential facilities and factories, leaving 1,500 megawatts for residents and raising daily public electricity supply to six to eight hours; Ahmed said the electricity then available covered only 40 percent of demand, leaving a 60 percent shortfall, and that no date had been established for production to resume. Rudaw's article image assets for that report are dated Nov 13, 2026. 964media, in a Nov 15 report, quoted Ahmed as saying that no timeframe had been set for supplies to return to normal and that within 48 hours of the attack generation had been increased from 1,000 megawatts to nearly 1,650 megawatts. Dana Gas, in a Nov 14 clarification later restated in coverage including a Kurdistan24 report, said the facility had sustained significant damage and that no gas could currently be produced. The Insight International, in a Nov 21 report citing private-generator officials who spoke to Rudaw on Saturday, Nov 21, said the public grid remained weak because of the gas shortfall and that neighborhood generators were still running for most of the day in Erbil, Sulaimani, and Duhok. No official customer count was given. No later official confirmation that Khor Mor production had already resumed was found as of 6:00 AM CT Wednesday, Nov 25 (3:00 p.m. Wednesday, Iraq time).
outages.etr: No official firm restoration time was given. The New Region, in a Nov 23, 2026 report, said Dana Gas was set to resume gas production in the next two to three days after a positive Monday meeting, that a source at the field said production was expected to resume within the next 48 hours in areas unaffected by the attack, and that Omed Ahmed, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Region's electricity ministry, said electricity generation at power stations was expected to resume within hours of gas production restarting, though it could take up to 24 hours of normal operations to return to pre-attack electricity-production levels. As of those reports, Khor Mor production had not been confirmed as having already resumed. No later official confirmation that production had already resumed was found as of 6:00 AM CT Wednesday, Nov 25 (3:00 p.m. Wednesday, Iraq time).

outages.place: Donetsk, Makiivka, Mariupol, Yenakiieve, Snizhne, Torez, and nearby districts, including Kirovskyi, Yasynuvata, Volodarske, and Amvrosiivka
outages.cause: Attacks on energy infrastructure, including a massive attack on the night of Nov 22, 2026, according to occupation officials, who said attacks on energy facilities were repeated the following night and that new outages were added to the effects of earlier damage. Occupation officials also described a power deficit and forced temporary outages to prevent accidents. Lenta novostei Donetska, in a Wednesday morning, Nov 25 report citing the occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy, said some of the remaining emergency outages were caused by damage to transmission lines, including damage from UAV attacks, and that a shortage of available capacity in the energy system could lead to temporary forced outages throughout Nov 25
outages.affected: Lenta novostei Donetska, in a report published at 8:36 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (11:36 p.m. CT Tuesday, Nov 24, if Moscow time), and DNR News, in a report published at 8:13 a.m. Wednesday (11:13 p.m. CT Tuesday if Moscow time), both citing the occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy, said planned repair and restoration work that the ministry had previously warned about had been completed only on the morning of Nov 25, that some consumers had been reconnected by 6:00 p.m., that remaining work continued overnight, and that by 6:00 a.m. electricity had been restored to all subscribers who had been without power because of the planned measures. Those same reports said not all electricity-supply problems had been eliminated and that local outages remained in some districts. According to operational data as of 6:00 a.m., more than 42,000 household subscribers remained without electricity. The reports said partial outages in Donetsk affected the Voroshylovskyi, Kalininskyi, Kyivskyi, and Kuibyshevskyi districts; that supply problems remained in the Hornyatskyi and Sovetskyi districts of Makiivka; that some consumers in the Zhovtnevyi district of Mariupol remained without electricity; and that outages were also recorded in the Yenakiieve, Snizhne, Torez, Kirovskyi, Yasynuvata, Volodarske, and Amvrosiivka municipal districts. Lenta novostei Donetska, citing the ministry, said some of the emergency outages were caused by damage to transmission lines, including damage from UAV attacks, that emergency crews had begun restoring the networks, and that energy workers expected to complete the main work during the course of Wednesday. The same reports said a shortage of available capacity in the energy system created additional difficulties, and that temporary forced outages were possible throughout Nov 25 in order to reduce the load on equipment and prevent new accidents. No later official customer count was found as of 6:00 AM CT Wednesday, Nov 25 (3:00 p.m. Wednesday if Moscow time).
outages.start: Night of Sunday, Nov 22, 2026, local time, for the attack described by occupation officials; occupation officials said attacks on energy facilities were repeated the following night; a further failure at about 11:00 p.m. Monday, Nov 23, was reported on Tuesday morning; other partial outages in the region were already being reported
outages.etr: Lenta novostei Donetska, in a report published at 8:36 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (11:36 p.m. CT Tuesday, Nov 24, if Moscow time), citing the occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy, said energy workers expected to complete the main restoration work on remaining damaged lines during the course of Wednesday, Nov 25; that was not a firm restoration time for the overall outage, and the same reports said temporary forced outages were possible throughout Nov 25 because of a shortage of available capacity. An earlier statement by occupation government head Andrei Chertkov, as reported by Lenta novostei Donetska at 9:06 p.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (12:06 p.m. CT if Moscow time), had said that if the situation developed favorably, a gradual reconnection of household subscribers disconnected for Tuesday's repair work would begin after 11:00 p.m.; the Wednesday morning ministry accounts said those planned-repair disconnections had been restored by 6:00 a.m., while more than 42,000 household subscribers remained without electricity for other reasons. An earlier Sunday statement by Chertkov, as reported by DNR News at 5:45 p.m. Sunday, Nov 22 (8:45 a.m. CT if Moscow time), had said restoration of the damaged energy center would take roughly two to three weeks

outages.place: Crimea, including Sevastopol, Yalta, Feodosia, Yevpatoria, Saky, Armyansk, and Dzhankoy, and Nyzhnohirskyi, Saky, Sovietskyi, Chornomorskyi, Krasnoperekopsk, Bakhchysarai, Kirovskyi, and Rozdolne districts
outages.cause: A power-capacity shortage after strikes on transmission networks outside the peninsula, according to occupation sources, and emergency repair work cited by occupation authorities as the reason for temporary supply restrictions beginning Wednesday, Nov 25. Krymenergo, as reported Wednesday morning by RIA Novosti Crimea, said temporary restrictions on electricity supply had been introduced from Nov 25, 2026, in connection with emergency work in Crimea, with an approximate duration of the restriction regime of up to 10 days and an approximate duration of one outage of three to six hours a day. Sergei Aksenov, the occupation head of Crimea, had said Tuesday that beginning Wednesday, for a period of no more than 10 days, electricity supply would be restricted, with a planned 30 percent reduction in capacity from 8:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. and the peak of outages from 12:00 p.m. to 3:00 p.m., and that there would be no restrictions from 9:00 p.m. to 8:00 a.m.; RIA Novosti said those hours were Moscow time. Sevastopol occupation governor Mikhail Razvozhaev had announced similar restrictions, according to the same RIA Novosti Crimea report
outages.affected: RIA Novosti Crimea, in a report published at 8:21 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25, and updated at 8:34 a.m. Wednesday (11:21 p.m. and 11:34 p.m. CT Tuesday, Nov 24, if Moscow time), citing Krymenergo in the MAX messenger, said temporary restrictions on electricity supply had been introduced from Nov 25, 2026, in connection with emergency work in Crimea, that the approximate period of the restrictions was up to 10 days, and that the duration of one outage was approximately three to six hours a day. The same report said that from Wednesday morning, electricity supply had been cut in hundreds of settlements in Nyzhnohirskyi, Saky, Sovietskyi, Chornomorskyi, Krasnoperekopsk, and Bakhchysarai districts; that there was also no electricity in dozens of villages in Dzhankoy district and partly in Dzhankoy itself; that Armyansk and Feodosia were partly without electricity; and that restrictions were also in effect on Wednesday morning in several districts of the Yevpatoria urban district and on dozens of streets in Yalta. Krymenergo, as reported by RIA Novosti Crimea, said a current list of settlements subject to the restrictions was being published on the enterprise's official resources, that socially significant facilities in Crimea were operating normally, and that the load was being distributed evenly among municipalities. The same report, citing Sevastopolenergo, said the electricity arriving in Sevastopol was insufficient to supply it according to schedules, that supply to socially significant facilities, including hospitals, hydraulic facilities, and other important sites, was being provided, and that operators were regulating the load on the basis of changing conditions and dispatch commands, which precluded advance notification of consumers. Rossiyskaya Gazeta, in a report published at 8:38 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (11:38 p.m. CT Tuesday if Moscow time), said the restrictions had begun to apply at 6:50 a.m. Wednesday, that outages would last from three to six hours, that outages had already affected more than 200 settlements, and that 10 districts were partly de-energized, including Saky, Chornomorskyi, Bakhchysarai, Nyzhnohirskyi, Dzhankoy, Sovietskyi, Kirovskyi, Krasnoperekopsk, Armyansk, and Rozdolne, as well as five cities: Yalta, Feodosia, Saky, Yevpatoria, and Armyansk. The same Rossiyskaya Gazeta report said that in Sevastopol lights went out on some streets at 7:00 a.m., that Sevenergo had first said a two-hours-on, six-hours-off schedule would be used, with four queues of consumers to be rotated during the day, but that the company later said the power arriving in the city was insufficient to distribute according to rolling schedules, that electricity would be switched off and on as possible, and that most of Sevastopol was de-energized, while water-utility facilities, hospitals, and other vital sites were being supplied, and some boiler houses, schools, and kindergartens in Sevastopol were connected to generators. No official customer count was found as of 6:00 AM CT Wednesday, Nov 25 (3:00 p.m. Wednesday if Moscow time).

outages.cause: Planned electricity restrictions that Tavanir said began Sunday, Nov 22, 2026, because fuel shortages were disrupting power generation
outages.affected: Al Jazeera, in a Nov 25, 2026 feature, said Iran was rationing electricity and described scheduled power cuts that officials had announced this week because fuel shortages were disrupting generation. Nour News, in a report published at 3:35 p.m. Tuesday, 3 Azar 1405 (6:05 a.m. CT Tuesday, Nov 24, if Iran time), on Wednesday, Nov 25 (4 Azar 1405) outages in Tehran, said a review of available notices found no confirmed public timetable that specified outage hours for all Tehran neighborhoods, and that customers should check the status of their subscription in the Bargh Man system, because timing could differ by area and subscription. The National, in an article dated November 23, 2026, and marked updated at 5:00 a.m., said scheduled cuts had begun and quoted Tavanir CEO Mohammad Allahdad as saying the restrictions may take the form of a two-hour outage over two days, or a maximum of two hours each day if temperatures fall, and quoted President Masoud Pezeshkian, via Isna, on expected winter difficulties. Euronews Persian, in a report dated 7:42 a.m. GMT+1 Monday, Nov 23 (12:42 a.m. CT Monday), said planned electricity outages began on Sunday, Nov 22 (1 Azar 1405), that Tavanir had announced the cuts on Saturday because of fuel-supply limitations at power plants, and that electricity-industry officials in Khorasan Razavi, Qazvin, and Kermanshah had confirmed the start of the restrictions. The same Euronews report, citing Mashhad distribution-company spokesman Majid Hassan-Nejad, said each outage turn in Mashhad would last two hours, though it was not yet clear whether the restrictions would be applied daily or with a gap of several days; citing Qazvin distribution-company official Seyed Mohammad Ghaflabashi, that household and commercial customers there were subject to the restrictions; and, citing Mehr news agency and Kermanshah distribution-company CEO Seyed Hamed Hosseini, that two-hour outages in Kermanshah were being applied between 9:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. Iran International, in a report dated 1:17 p.m. GMT Sunday, Nov 22 (7:17 a.m. CT), said scheduled cuts were resuming and that Sunday reports from Tehran, Isfahan, Shiraz, Mashhad, Yazd, Kermanshah, and Ardabil described hours-long outages, often without notice, and quoted Allahdad on restrictions beginning Nov 22 because of fuel shortages. Nour News, in a report dated 8:09 a.m. Iran time Sunday, Nov 22, or 1 Azar 1405 (10:39 p.m. CT Saturday), and Eghtesad Online, in a report dated 8:29 a.m. Iran time Sunday (10:59 p.m. CT Saturday) that cited Nour News, said planned electricity restrictions began that day and, citing the Tavanir chief executive, that the new restrictions may take the form of a two-hour outage over two days, or a maximum of two hours each day, that the timing is not fixed and may change with network conditions, and that customers would be informed through the Bargh-e Man system and app, the Bale messenger app, and text messages. Tavanir had announced on Saturday, Nov 21, that planned electricity restrictions on households and businesses would begin on Sunday, Nov 22, because fuel shortages were disrupting power generation, according to Iran International in a report dated 5:11 p.m. GMT Saturday, Nov 21 (11:11 a.m. CT), and to RFE/RL. Anar News, in a report updated at 12:05 a.m. UTC Sunday, Nov 22 (6:05 p.m. CT Saturday), citing BBC Persian, also said planned power outages began in Iran on Sunday, Nov 22, because of fuel shortages at power plants. No official nationwide customer count was found as of 6:00 AM CT Wednesday, Nov 25 (3:30 p.m. Wednesday, Iran time).

outages.cause: Drone attacks on power stations and other electricity infrastructure during the war between the Rapid Support Forces and the Sudanese Armed Forces
outages.affected: No official customer count. Drop Site News, in a Nov 20, 2026 report from Khartoum, said a particularly intense wave of drone strikes at the end of October and into November targeting power stations, fuel supplies, and electricity infrastructure had brought the country's power grid to the brink of collapse, and that two weeks after the wave of attacks, major substations remained out of service. Shaker Ismail, an engineer with the Sudanese Electricity Company, told Drop Site that repairing some of the country's most important power facilities could take months or longer, that high-capacity transformers and digital control systems had been damaged, and that replacement transformers must be manufactured to order abroad. Ismail said the Um Dabakir thermal power plant in White Nile State was badly damaged in an Oct 29 strike and forced to shut down, and that the Al-Markhiyat substation west of Omdurman was put out of service after an Oct 27 strike; he said affected areas continued to experience prolonged outages and scheduled power cuts as of this week. The report said the Sudan Electricity Holding Company and Ministry of Energy had yet to publicly announce the restoration of the major facilities damaged in the attacks. A United Nations report published Nov 17, issued in Geneva and posted on the UN in Sudan website, said that in just over two weeks between Oct 20 and Nov 4, 29 drone strikes, attributed to the Rapid Support Forces, hit electricity facilities and fuel stations across 11 states, triggering widespread power blackouts and further fuel shortages affecting millions far from the conflict frontlines. An earlier Al Jazeera Nov 15 feature said there is no clear schedule for the resulting power cuts, which can last anywhere between six hours and a day, and, citing The Associated Press, said repeated drone attacks on power stations have seen electricity generation fall from about 4,400 megawatts before the war to about 1,100 MW. Residents and a small-business owner in Port Sudan described prolonged, unreliable cuts, including outages lasting more than 24 hours. Al-Ghad Al-Sudani, in a report last updated Nov 22, 2026, said explosions and drone flights returned to Khartoum on Sunday morning, Nov 22, amid reports of attacks on military sites in various parts of the capital, and that the attacks coincided with power outages in large parts of the city; the report did not give a customer count or independently establish the cause of that outage. Democracy Now, in a Nov 24, 2026 headline, said Sudan's military reported intercepting drones launched by the Rapid Support Forces over Khartoum after attacks that struck the city's main airport and several buildings, including a U.N. facility, and that those attacks came as Sudan's power grid was on the brink of collapse following attacks on electricity stations; that headline did not state that the Nov 24 drone activity itself had struck power stations or give a customer count. No later official national customer count or official restoration timetable was found as of 6:00 AM CT Wednesday, Nov 25 (2:00 p.m. Wednesday, Sudan time).
